The Sahara Desert. The world's largest hot desert, spanning roughly three point six million square miles across North Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea. Its harsh climate and vast expanses historically shaped migration patterns, trade routes, and the development of African civilizations, from ancient kingdoms to modern cities built around oases.

It stretches across eleven North African countries, including Egypt, Libya, Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, and Sudan. Temperatures regularly exceed fifty degrees Celsius, or one hundred and twenty-two degrees Fahrenheit, during summer. Nights can drop near freezing due to the lack of atmospheric moisture.

The Sahel region to its south marks its semi-arid boundary, a critical zone for drought, desertification, and climatic variation. The Rub al-Khali, the Empty Quarter, is one of its largest continuous sand expanses. Another massive sand sea is the Erg Chech.

The Sahara supports oasis settlements like Timbuktu and Gao, which became centers of medieval Islamic scholarship and trans-Saharan commerce. The desert is expanding southward at roughly forty-eight kilometers per decade, a process called desertification, driven by overgrazing and climate change. Salt mining occurs in places like Taoudenni, Mali, where salt was traded across medieval Africa as a luxury commodity.

The Nile River serves as the lifeline of Egypt on the Sahara's eastern edge. Mali, Songhai, and Kanem-Bornu controlled trans-Saharan trade routes. Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire and crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca. The Roman Empire controlled the Sahara's northern coast, with the desert marking its southern boundary. Islam in Africa spread southward via merchants and traders crossing the Sahara, making it the cultural and commercial bridge between the Mediterranean and sub-Saharan Africa.
